questions.prompt: How does a state differ from a trait?
questions.answer: A state refers to a particular occasion; a trait describes broader tendencies across occasions.

questions.prompt: Can equal averages hide different behavioural distributions?
questions.answer: Yes; variation, range and context patterns may differ.
questions.feedback: Show an example from the synthetic data.

questions.answer: Unequal roles, duration or access can confound raw behaviour counts.

questions.prompt: Does situational variation contradict the existence of traits?
questions.answer: Not necessarily; characteristic distributions can coexist with substantial variation.
questions.feedback: Avoid assuming every occasion is identical.

scoring.knowledge: 1 point per correct answer; formative only. Use answer-specific feedback and delayed retest.
scoring.practice: Compares fictional behavioural distributions and contextual conditions, calculates descriptive summaries and avoids unsupported stable-trait claims.
scoring.transfer: Construct a fictional six-observation dataset for a different behaviour, with two contexts and equal observation windows. Summarise average, range and contextual variation. Identify why the pattern may not generalise and how a better sampling design could reduce uncertainty.
scoring.pass: All mapped criteria require Level 2 evidence; no averaging away omissions or safety-critical criteria. No automatic competency award.
